verses.text: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God.
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;
And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.
For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.
For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die.
But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.
For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.
And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement.
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
( For until the law sin was in the world: but sin is not imputed when there is no law.
Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come.

But not as the offence, so also is the free gift. For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many.
And not as it was by one that sinned, so is the gift: for the judgment was by one to condemnation, but the free gift is of many offences unto justification.
For if by one man’s offence death reigned by one; much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ.)
Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life.
For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound:
That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord.

summary: Paul draws the consequence of everything argued so far with a single word, "Therefore," and states the result: "being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." Justification is not left as a verdict filed away; it opens a door, for "by whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God." That standing turns even affliction into ground for boasting: "we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope." The chain does not end in wishful thinking, because "hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us" — the love is poured in, not merely announced. Paul then proves that love from its timing rather than from our worthiness: "when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly," and where "scarcely for a righteous man will one die," "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Twice he argues from the greater to the greater still — "Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him," and "if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life" — so that the death reconciles and the risen life saves. The present result is joy: "we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement." From verse twelve the argument widens to the whole race. "As by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned," and the proof that sin is deeper than any statute is that "death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression." Adam is therefore "the figure of him that was to come," a likeness broken by asymmetry: "not as the offence, so also is the free gift," for "the judgment was by one to condemnation, but the free gift is of many offences unto justification." Where one offence let death reign, "they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ" — reigning, not merely surviving. The parallel is stated twice in full, once in terms of act — "as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life" — and once in terms of person and will: "as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." The law's entrance did not reverse the ruin but exposed it, "that the offence might abound"; yet exposure is overwhelmed by gift, "where sin abounded, grace did much more abound." The chapter closes with two reigns and only one survivor: "as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord."
takeaways: Peace with God is described as an accomplished state rather than a mood: "we have peace with God" and "we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand." The verbs are of position and entry, so justification is presented as admission into a standing place, not only as a charge dismissed.

The love of God is not merely reported to the believer but placed inside him — "shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us" — which is why suffering can produce hope rather than cynicism. Tribulation refines what has already been poured in; it does not manufacture it.

Paul grounds assurance in chronology, not in self-assessment. Christ died "when we were yet without strength" and "while we were yet sinners," so the worst possible moment has already been survived, and the twin "much more" arguments reason from the harder thing accomplished to the easier thing promised.

Adam and Christ are set as two heads of one race, and the comparison is deliberately unequal. One offence brought condemnation upon all, but the gift answers "many offences unto justification," so grace is not a repair returning us to the starting line but an overflow that ends in reigning "in life by one, Jesus Christ."

The law is given a diagnostic role, entering "that the offence might abound," which makes it the servant of grace rather than its rival. The final image is governmental — sin "reigned unto death," grace reigns "through righteousness unto eternal life" — so salvation is a change of sovereignty, not merely a change of record.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 3 — by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin
crossRefs.why: Paul's whole argument from verse twelve rests on the garden narrative, where a single act of disobedience brings exile and mortality upon the race. Reading them together shows why he treats death as an intruder with a history rather than as a natural fact, and why the remedy must also come through one man's act.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 — as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive
crossRefs.why: Paul states the same two-head typology elsewhere and there completes it with resurrection, calling Christ "the last Adam." It confirms that "we shall be saved by his life" in this chapter is not a figure of speech but points to the risen life the believer is destined to share.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 2:5-11 — obedient unto death, even the death of the cross
crossRefs.why: Romans 5 hinges on "the obedience of one" without describing it, and this hymn supplies the content: a self-emptying obedience carried to the cross and answered by exaltation. Set beside verse nineteen, it shows that what undoes Adam's disobedience is a whole life of obedient self-gift, not merely a legal transaction at the end of it.

crossRefs.label: Romans 6:1-14 — shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid
crossRefs.why: Paul raises this question precisely because "where sin abounded, grace did much more abound" invites it, and he answers with baptism into Christ's death and resurrection. The next chapter is the intended safeguard against reading Romans 5 as permission, and it turns the reign of grace into a summons to walk "in newness of life."

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:31-39 — who shall separate us from the love of Christ?
crossRefs.why: The later chapter expands both halves of Romans 5: the Spirit given to us, and the argument from the greater to the greater — if God "spared not his own Son," how shall he not also give us all things? It shows that the confidence begun in "hope maketh not ashamed" is meant to widen, and that tribulation reappears there as something already conquered.

crossRefs.label: James 1:2-4 — the trying of your faith worketh patience
crossRefs.why: James builds the same chain from trial to endurance to maturity, using nearly the same vocabulary, which shows the pattern of Romans 5:3-4 was common apostolic teaching rather than a private flourish. Together they present suffering as formative under grace, aiming at a completed character rather than at mere survival.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes justification in this chapter as a real interior renewal and not only a change of legal standing. The text does not stop at a verdict but speaks of entry — "access by faith into this grace wherein we stand" — and of love genuinely poured in, "the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us." On this reading "shall many be made righteous" means actually made so by grace received, the faith that justifies is a living faith that works through charity, and what begins in justification continues as growth in that same grace rather than as a separate process running alongside an unchanged verdict.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters classically read "justified by faith" as a forensic declaration: God pronounces the believer righteous on the ground of Christ's obedience reckoned to him, and "made righteous" in verse nineteen means constituted righteous in standing, parallel to the way Adam's one offence constituted many sinners before any of them had acted. The strength of the reading is the chapter's own courtroom vocabulary of condemnation, judgment, and justification, and its insistence that the gift comes "while we were yet sinners" — before any renewal could be alleged as its cause. Sanctification is then held to be inseparable from justification but distinct from it, so that the believer's transformation is the certain fruit of the verdict rather than part of its basis. Both traditions affirm that grace is entirely unmerited, that Christ's work is the sole ground of acceptance, and that no one is left unchanged by it.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats the confidence of "we shall be saved from wrath through him" as a firm and joyful hope rather than an absolute certainty of final perseverance. The chapter's own grammar is future and expectant — believers "rejoice in hope of the glory of God," and hope is what "maketh not ashamed" — so the tradition holds that one may have real and well-founded confidence in God's fidelity while still needing to persevere, since grace received into a standing place can be abandoned by grave sin and is restored by repentance.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the two "much more" arguments as guarantees rather than encouragements: if God acted for enemies at the cost of his Son's death, the lesser thing — keeping the reconciled — is secure, and the believer may rest in that. In the Reformed strand this supports the perseverance of the saints, with assurance treated as a proper fruit of faith rather than presumption. Other Protestant traditions, notably the Wesleyan and Arminian, hold that grace can be resisted and forsaken, standing closer to the Catholic reading on this point. Both traditions agree that the ground of confidence is Christ's finished work and never the believer's own strength, and that presumption and despair are equally foreign to the chapter.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds original sin in verse twelve — sin entering "by one man" so that "death passed upon all men" — as a condition contracted by descent rather than merely imitated, a real deprivation of the grace and holiness in which humanity was meant to stand. On this reading baptism truly removes that sin, while the disordered inclination that remains afterward is the residue and occasion of sin but is not itself sin in the proper sense until it is consented to.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters likewise read the verse as teaching a fallen condition inherited by all, and many press it further, taking Adam's guilt to be imputed to his descendants on the strength of the parallel with the one righteousness imputed in verses eighteen and nineteen. The Reformation traditions also differ on what remains after baptism, holding that the persisting concupiscence is genuinely sin even when unconsented, which is why the believer is described as continually needing forgiveness. Both traditions affirm that the ruin is universal and prior to individual choice, that no one repairs it from within, and that the whole force of the chapter is that the remedy in Christ exceeds the damage in Adam.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
